issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: 'Talking about the future' is a weak and atypical trigger for a life-threatening accident in this profile, and it lacks a clear clinical link to the rest of the selected memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other triggers are interpersonal/victim-related, but this item suggests a different theme that is not supported elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'Checking if someone is following me' implies pursuit/interpersonal threat. In a life-threatening accident profile, this is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report, which otherwise reflects generalized danger, hypervigilance, and trauma-memory disturbance rather than a specific persecutory/following threat.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a 58-year-old fisherman with a life-threatening accident, 'Reminders of victims' implies exposure to multiple casualties or dead/injured others. That is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reads like a personal survival-focused accident trauma rather than a mass-casualty/witnessing-victims presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by disorganized, present-tense reliving ('Cannot Find Words', 'Feels Present Not Past'), which fits severe PTSD, but 'intense rage' on recall points to a qualitatively different emotional tone that is not supported elsewhere by the triggers, threat, or appraisals. With no corroborating anger/blame themes, this item stands out as internally and cross-node incongruent.

vignette: Arjun, a 58-year-old fisherman of South Asian descent, has lived most of his life on the waters off the Gulf Coast, his days punctuated by the creak of a boat and the rhythm of the tide. In late summer of 2018, when the sea was unusually calm, a sudden collision with a passing cargo ship shattered his routine. The boom of metal, the splash of seawater, and the deafening crash left him clutching a torn piece of hull while his body convulsed in panic. In the minutes that followed, he could not recall the words that should have guided him; he knew the event was there, but he could not find the language to describe it. Since then, every time a stranger approaches his dock or a new face enters his small town, he feels that same surge of terror, as if the memory is pulling him back into the instant of the wreck. These stranger interactions have become potent triggers that, instantly, evoke the visceral image of a car-his fishing vessel-hit by an unseen force, reminding him of the collision and sending the scene back into the present. Arjun's distrust of others now runs deeper than mere caution. The very act of speaking to strangers, even to a fisherman who offers a friendly nod, feels like a betrayal because he believes people are not what they seem. That belief fuels a heightened sense of threat: the silence that follows a conversation feels like a prelude to danger, and his body, once a reliable tool for hauling nets, now seems deceptive. His constant scanning for danger in the low light of his own home, the way he holds his breath when the wind shifts, is a direct expression of that threat. The belief that his body can no longer be trusted compels him to keep a rigid guard even inside his modest dwelling, and he often finds himself staring at the shadow of a curtain, convinced that a hidden danger lurks. The terror that floods Arjun's mind whenever he recalls the wreck is almost as intense as the terror he felt at the moment of impact. Each recollection feels present, as if the crash is happening again, and the fear is so profound that he is convinced his life is in imminent peril. This terror on recall is not simply a flashback; it reshapes his sense of self. He no longer recognizes himself, because the identity that once thrived on the ocean's rhythm is now eclipsed by the image of a shattered hull and a trembling body. That identity loss reinforces his distrust and heightens his perception of threat, creating a loop where every memory of the event feeds back into the cycle of fear and suspicion. When he feels the sting of danger in his own home, the same image of the collision resurfaces, and the memory reasserts its presence, pulling him further into his protective shell. In his current work, Arjun has begun to avoid venturing beyond the familiar reef, steering clear of any vessel that does not match his own. He now refuses to accept passengers on his boat, fearing the strangers who might board could betray him. The constant threat he perceives-whether in the hush of a crowded dock or the quiet of his cabin-makes him retreat from the community that once provided him companionship. The body unreliability he feels has led him to avoid the physical exertions that once defined his identity, and his sense of self erodes further with each missed haul. The memory of the crash, the feeling that it is always present, and the belief that he cannot trust those around him and even his own body have become the scaffolding that supports the relentless threat that governs his day. It is this unrelenting cycle-triggers that summon the memory, memory that stokes negative appraisals, and appraisals that elevate threat-that has driven Arjun to seek help. He has come to believe that without an intervention he will continue to live in a state of constant alert, unable to enjoy the simple peace of his own home or the camaraderie of his fellow fishermen. His most pressing fear is that the memory will never let him rest, that the terror on recall will persist until he loses the one thing that still grounds him: his sense of self and his trust in his own body. Yet he holds a fragile hope that, through understanding and treatment, he might reclaim the voice he lost after the crash and find a way to let the sea's rhythm flow through him once more.
